title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
story_key: Anthropic: FlashProve zkSNARK provable inference prototype
summary: Anthropic researchers present FlashProve, an open-source system based on zero-knowledge succinct proofs (zkSNARKs) that would let a model provider commit to a model and prove each response came from it, without revealing the weights. Their benchmark on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B mixture-of-experts model, 4-bit quantized) reports about 110 tokens/second per H100 GPU, roughly 19 MB of proof per 1,024-token request, and about 70-95x the GPU time of running the model on vLLM. They also release a fast C++ verifier and Lean formal proofs of the top-level security claims. The figures are the authors' own and not yet independently replicated, and they describe the work as intermediate progress.
why_it_matters: If you route LLM calls through third parties or need to verify which model served a response, this points to a future option, but at the current overhead it is a research prototype rather than something to adopt within months.

title: Make long-running agents faster with message threads
story_key: Claude Platform: message threads public beta
summary: Anthropic has released message threads in public beta on the Claude Platform. With a thread, agents send only new messages and the previous response ID each turn instead of resending the full conversation, which the post says cuts time to first token for long sessions. The post reports a median TTFT drop of about 35% for requests of 500k to 1M tokens in Claude Code, where the feature is on by default for most users. Token usage stays the same because Claude still reads the full conversation each turn, and a thread expires 5 minutes after its last request.
why_it_matters: If I build long-running Claude agents, I can cut latency by threading requests instead of resending full histories, though I need to plan for the 5-minute expiry and the unchanged token cost.

why_it_matters: If you rely on LLMs to follow evolving state across long documents or chained updates, this suggests you should test those pipelines on long inputs rather than assume reliable tracking, and the architecture findings are a long-term signal for model choice.

title: Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems
story_key: Route Anything: model and policy routing study across general-purpose AI systems
summary: The authors built a test set of 374,401 scored runs from 452 model and policy configurations across 25 benchmarks (language, image, video, speech, coding agents, and robot manipulation). Per-input oracle routing beats the best single fixed candidate by 5.4 points, and learned routers beat it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks. The paper reports 8.82x average efficiency gains over a reference model, but the text does not explain how that figure was measured. This is a single arXiv preprint with moderate early attention (87 upvotes), so treat the numbers as a lab's claims until others reproduce them.
why_it_matters: If you build with LLMs such as Claude, it suggests that routing requests across models by cost and quality is a practical lever for lowering spend, though the learned-router gains here are modest and the benefit is a medium-term design consideration rather than an immediate change.

summary: Snowflake announced new CoWork capabilities: Profiles, which route user questions to the right agent without the user choosing one, and Snowflake Dashboards (public preview), which the agent can discuss and query against the governed data behind them. Automations run recurring tasks on a schedule using the user's own permissions, and some can take actions such as creating a Jira ticket or sending a Slack message. Most of the other capabilities are generally available, and Cortex AI Gateway for model access governance is in public preview. The announcement is vendor-written and the Dashboard feature is still in preview.
why_it_matters: It shows a competing BI platform moving toward conversational, agent-driven dashboards on governed data, a direction Fabric and Power BI will be measured against, though it does not change anything I can use today.

title: Snowflake CoCo: Autonomous Cloud Agents for Data Work
story_key: Snowflake CoCo: autonomous Cloud Agents, automations and Cortex Agent SDK GA
summary: Snowflake announced updates to its CoCo agent: Cloud Agents that keep running long sessions after the user leaves, plus automations that run recurring jobs on a schedule or webhook under the creator's permissions. Several pieces are stated as generally available (skills and plugin sharing, the Cortex Agent SDK in Python and TypeScript) while memory, dynamic model routing and MCP connector management via Cortex AI Gateway Tools are in public preview. The post is largely promotional and includes no independent benchmarks or customer evidence.
why_it_matters: For someone building LLM agents, the GA Cortex Agent SDK and the scheduled-automation pattern are a concrete reference for running unattended agent work, though this only matters directly if Snowflake is in your stack.

title: Business Ontology: Governed Context for AI | Snowflake
story_key: Snowflake announces Business Ontology (public preview soon)
summary: Snowflake announced Business Ontology, a governance layer in Horizon Context where teams define business concepts, metrics and their relationships, with owners and approval status, linked to the semantic views and tables that implement them. Only approved definitions are served to AI agents in CoCo and CoWork, and definitions can be imported and exported via open formats (Apache Ossie, RDF). The feature is announced as public preview 'soon', and much of the text is vendor positioning and partner quotes.
why_it_matters: For a Fabric and Power BI shop building LLM agents, it signals that business definitions may increasingly live in a governed, shared layer separate from any single semantic model, which is worth tracking against your own semantic model and metric governance design.

title: Introducing Apache Spark® 4.3 - Now available in Databricks Runtime 19
story_key: Apache Spark 4.3 adds stateful Real-Time Mode
summary: Apache Spark 4.3, available in Databricks Runtime 19, extends Structured Streaming's low-latency Real-Time Mode to stateful operations such as streaming aggregations, deduplication and custom transformWithState. The blog reports sub-150 ms P99 end-to-end latency on three tested stateful workloads, which it describes as measurements rather than a guarantee. The release also moves Spark to a quarterly feature-release cadence and adds opt-in optimizations for small-data exploration.
why_it_matters: Stateful low-latency streaming within the familiar Structured Streaming APIs could remove the need for a separate streaming engine for some millisecond-scale use cases, which matters if you evaluate streaming options alongside Fabric or Power BI workloads.

title: Unify operational and Lakehouse data with direct Iceberg access in AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
story_key: AlloyDB: direct Iceberg access in preview, sync and Lakehouse federation GA
summary: Google announced direct Iceberg access in AlloyDB for PostgreSQL in preview, letting applications query Apache Iceberg tables in Cloud Storage and join them with live operational data in one SQL query. It also made AlloyDB sync (copying BigQuery data into AlloyDB on a schedule) and Lakehouse federation (querying native BigQuery tables in place) generally available. Google's own tests report up to 7x faster aggregations than Amazon's comparable PostgreSQL-compatible service on a 1 TB dataset, but these are vendor-run benchmarks.
why_it_matters: It offers a way to join Iceberg history with operational data inside a Postgres database without building pipelines, which is relevant to architecture choices for data products, though it sits outside the Fabric/Power BI stack.

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro model weights are out
story_key: Moonshot releases Kimi K3.1 Pro open weights
summary: Moonshot AI released the weights of Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face, describing it as an open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model in the 3T-parameter class and the first model in the K3.1 series. It is post-trained from Kimi K3 with large-scale reinforcement learning and has a 1-million-token context window. Compared with K3, it swaps full-attention layers for Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention to make long-context processing more efficient. The performance gains it claims are vendor-reported benchmark results, not independently verified.
why_it_matters: An open-weight model with a 1M-token context and agentic coding claims gives a Fabric/Power BI team building with LLMs another self-hostable or low-cost option to evaluate against Claude for agent and coding workloads.

The company reports a score of 80.52 on TerminalBench 2.1, which it says is the top result among U.S. open-weight models on agentic coding, and says the model was trained for about $32M. why_it_matters: If the agentic coding benchmark results hold up under independent testing, this is another open-weight option for self-hosted coding agents that the company says can run on local hardware like the DGX Spark.

title: [AINews] Behind Latent Space: Kill My SaaS, Jev & AI in 2026 | AIEi Shanghai
story_key: Weight-space programming: frontier LLMs editing neural network weights directly
summary: Several groups report that frontier LLMs can write or edit the weights of small neural networks directly, without gradient training or tools, following an MIT experiment. Hugging Face reproduced the paper, and a Zhihu reconstruction says a headline gain on Qwen3.5-0.8B mostly comes from fixing looping outputs rather than new reasoning. Critics say the claims lack competent baselines and the benchmark results may be overfitted, so the solidity is mixed.
why_it_matters: If models can reliably edit weights, it could change how one fine-tunes or patches small models, but for a Fabric/Power BI team building with Claude this is a research signal to watch rather than something to adopt within months.

title: [AINews] It's Swapping Season
story_key: Kimi K3.1 Pro open weights release
summary: Moonshot released open weights for its flagship Kimi K3.1 Pro, described by Modal as a post-training update to K3 with expanded reinforcement learning for coding, financial research and long-horizon agentic work. The model accepts text and images and has a 1M-token context window, and it is hosted on Ollama Cloud, Databricks and SkyPilot. On Agent Arena, one independent ranking, it places first among open models and 13th overall. This item is a multi-story newsletter roundup, and the other stories in it (personnel moves, acquisitions, a research claim about sandbagging) were not kept.
why_it_matters: A strong open-weight agentic coding model with a 1M context that is already hosted on Databricks and Ollama Cloud gives a self-hosting or cheaper-hosting option worth evaluating against the LLM APIs used in current builds.

title: Salesforce Data 360 integration with OneLake (Preview)
story_key: Fabric: Salesforce Data 360 shortcuts to OneLake (Preview)
summary: Microsoft announced a public preview that lets Fabric users create OneLake table shortcuts to Salesforce Data 360 Data Lake Objects, so the data can be queried from lakehouses and warehouses without building an ingestion pipeline or copying it. The shortcuts reference the live data in Salesforce rather than importing a separate copy. During preview, only Data Lake Objects with the _dll extension are supported; Data Model Objects, Calculated Insight Objects and schema-level shortcuts are not.
why_it_matters: If your customer data sits in Salesforce Data 360, you can join it with Fabric data through shortcuts instead of maintaining a separate ingestion pipeline, though the preview scope is narrow.

title: Bring your Fabric data into your next app with connectors
story_key: Fabric Apps: connectors to Fabric data sources
summary: Microsoft's Fabric Updates blog describes connectors in Fabric Apps that let an application read, and for some sources create, update and delete, data in Fabric lakehouse SQL analytics endpoints, warehouses, SQL databases in Fabric, and Power BI semantic models. The post frames this with example scenarios (incident triage, seller 360, store operations) and shows a CLI command to add a read-only warehouse connector. Operations are scoped per connector, so a read-only app need not request write access.
why_it_matters: For a Fabric and Power BI shop, this offers a supported way to build operational apps directly on governed Fabric data and semantic models, instead of copying data into separate application stacks.

title: Govern Fabric connections with admin APIs and data connection policies (Preview)
story_key: Fabric: admin connection APIs and data connection policies (Preview)
summary: Microsoft describes two preview capabilities for governing Fabric connections. The admin connection APIs let tenant administrators list all tenant connections, including ones they do not own, and manage Owner role assignments, for example to hand a connection over when its owner leaves. Data connection policies, configured in the Fabric admin portal, include an authentication allowlist and a tenant allowlist that restrict which authentication methods and Microsoft Entra tenants cloud connections may use, and enforcement applies to existing connections as well as new ones. The article notes that granting Owner does not transfer OAuth credentials, and that enabling the allowlist can disrupt existing workflows.
why_it_matters: For a Fabric and Power BI estate, this gives a tenant-wide inventory of connections and a way to enforce authentication rules, but enabling the allowlist needs prior review of affected connections to avoid breaking pipelines.

title: OneLake table APIs: Now with Iceberg writes, plus richer table metadata (Preview)
story_key: OneLake table APIs: Iceberg REST Catalog writes GA, table metadata API preview
summary: Microsoft added Iceberg REST Catalog write operations to the OneLake table endpoint, so Iceberg-compatible clients such as PyIceberg, Snowflake and DuckDB can create native Iceberg tables, commit snapshots and get short-lived storage credentials. Commits use optimistic concurrency checks so conflicting updates fail rather than overwrite. A new table metadata API, in preview, lets users read and write descriptions and key-value tags on tables and columns, and the updates also apply through OneLake shortcuts.
why_it_matters: External engines can now land results directly into Fabric OneLake as Iceberg tables and the tables can carry business descriptions, which changes how I would architect data flows and semantic context for Fabric and Power BI.

title: Find expensive queries from Capacity Metrics (Generally Available)
story_key: Fabric: Capacity Metrics 'Monitor in warehouse' action GA
summary: The 'Monitor in warehouse' action in the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app is now generally available. It links a capacity usage spike (a timepoint) to a supported warehouse operation and opens Warehouse Monitor with that time window applied. The post also describes which query columns to check (CPU time, data scanned, result cache hit, distributed execution) and says the Data Warehouse operations skill in Skills for Fabric can correlate the two data sources with an AI prompt.
why_it_matters: For anyone running Fabric warehouses on a shared capacity, this shortens the path from a CU spike to the specific queries behind it, which is useful when tuning workloads or deciding on capacity sizing.

title: Eventhouse support for OneLake security (Generally Available)
story_key: Fabric: Eventhouse support for OneLake security GA
summary: Microsoft has made generally available OneLake security enforcement for Eventhouse external tables. KQL queries against OneLake data now automatically apply object-level, column-level and row-level access rules defined in OneLake security roles. The post says the Eventhouse endpoint for Lakehouses queries the data without creating another copy.
why_it_matters: If you expose Lakehouse data to KQL users through Eventhouse, you can now keep one centrally managed OneLake security model instead of recreating row and column rules for that path.
